lessons.summary: Distinguish fitness qualities and evaluate what a fictional measure can establish without treating a result as a health diagnosis.
objectives: Relate a fitness quality to a stated task.
Distinguish validity and reliability.
Identify limits of a proposed test or plan.
explanation: Fitness refers to capacities relevant to particular activities, rather than one score that ranks a whole person. Speed, strength, muscular endurance and cardiorespiratory endurance describe different demands. A measure chosen for one purpose may not answer a different question. The interpretation also depends on the conditions and on who the measure is suitable for. A classroom example of a test is not a request to attempt it.

Validity concerns whether evidence supports the intended interpretation; reliability concerns consistency under comparable conditions. A consistently recorded result can still be an unsuitable measure of the chosen quality. Real testing requires appropriate instruction, suitability and school guidance. The original fictional records here support discussion of measures and evidence only. They cannot diagnose health, certify safe technique or establish an individual training workload. Keep performance observations separate from assumptions about wellbeing or personal worth.
keyIdeas: Different activities make different demands.
Consistency does not guarantee validity.
A result needs context and an appropriate interpretation.

definitions.meaning: The extent to which evidence supports the intended interpretation of a measure.
Consistency under comparable measurement conditions.
Capacity to sustain activity supported by the circulatory and respiratory systems.

method: Name the stated activity demand.
Identify the quality the measure aims to describe.
Check comparable conditions and suitability information.
State what the result cannot establish.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional report uses a short sprint time as its only evidence that a learner can sustain a prolonged activity. Evaluate the interpretation.
steps: The timed sprint provides information about performance over that short distance.
Sustaining a prolonged activity involves demands not established by the short sprint alone.
Consistent timing does not remove that validity problem.
Identify relevant evidence with a qualified teacher rather than attempting a new test unsupervised.
workedExample.conclusion: The measure does not establish the broader endurance claim; further appropriate evidence would be needed.

misconceptions.mistake: One fitness score describes all capacities.
misconceptions.correction: Relate each measure to its intended task and interpretation.

misconceptions.mistake: Discomfort proves improvement.
misconceptions.correction: Discomfort is not evidence of improved capacity and should not be used as a target.

practice.prompt: A fictional task concerns covering a short distance quickly. Name a relevant fitness quality and explain why this does not establish prolonged endurance.
hints: Separate short-duration speed and sustained activity.
solution: Speed is relevant to covering the short distance quickly.
That performance alone does not establish ability to sustain a prolonged activity.

practice.prompt: Two fictional timings used different distances and different start signals. Explain why a smaller time does not by itself prove improvement.
hints: Check comparable conditions.
solution: Distance and starting procedure changed, so the times do not represent the same task under comparable conditions.
Use a defined, appropriate observation protocol and qualified guidance before interpreting a difference.

practice.prompt: A template claims one automatic percentage increase makes every exercise plan suitable for every learner. Evaluate without prescribing a replacement workload.
hints: Suitability depends on more than arithmetic.
solution: The claim ignores activity, experience, individual circumstances and recovery.
A percentage calculation does not establish safety or suitability.
Real plans require appropriate qualified review and a way to respond to concerns.

checklist: I connect a measure with a task.
I recognise the need for appropriate guidance.

lessons.summary: Explain specificity, training demand and recovery through fictional plan analysis while keeping individual workload decisions with appropriate guidance.
objectives: Identify frequency, intensity, time and type in a written example.
Explain specificity and recovery.
Recognise why a universal progression rule is insufficient.
explanation: Training principles describe relationships between activity demands, adaptation and recovery. Specificity means that changes depend on what is practised, so an activity should relate to the intended aim. Training load describes demand; it can be represented through measures such as duration or effort, but no single number captures every aspect. Adaptation and recovery differ across people and circumstances, so more demand does not automatically mean better learning or performance.

Frequency, intensity, time and type provide a way to describe a proposed activity. Identifying these components is a literacy task, not approval to perform the example. A real plan needs a suitable starting point, appropriate instruction, recovery and review of concerns. Progression should not be reduced to one universal percentage or a promise of safety. These original fictional cases teach analysis and clear records. They do not prescribe exercise, diagnose fatigue or certify an individual’s readiness.
keyIdeas: Activity choices should relate to the aim.
Demand and recovery both matter.
Describing a schedule does not establish its suitability.

definitions.meaning: The relationship between the activity practised and the adaptations or skills developed.
The demand created by activity, described using relevant measures.
Processes and conditions through which fatigue can reduce and adaptation can occur.

method: Identify the aim and activity described.
Label frequency, intensity, time and type.
Check missing context and review arrangements.
State limits without prescribing an individual change.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional worksheet: two 15-minute easy cycling sessions each week. Identify FITT and one limit of the record.
steps: Frequency is two sessions each week.
Intensity is described as easy, but the description is subjective.
Time is 15 minutes per session; type is cycling.
These labels do not establish suitability for a particular person or approve the schedule.
workedExample.conclusion: FITT describes the written example; individual participation needs appropriate guidance and context.

misconceptions.mistake: Maximum intensity is always best.
misconceptions.correction: The appropriate demand depends on the aim, person, activity and recovery.

misconceptions.mistake: A fixed progression rule applies to every learner.
misconceptions.correction: A rule cannot replace relevant context and qualified review.

practice.prompt: In a fictional worksheet, identify FITT in “three 30-minute easy cycling sessions each week”. Do not treat it as a recommended programme.
hints: Match each detail to its category.
solution: Frequency: three sessions per week.
Intensity: described as easy.
Time: 30 minutes per session.
Type: cycling.

practice.prompt: A fictional template increases duration, frequency and intensity together, then attributes the outcome only to duration. Explain the evidence problem.
hints: Several variables changed.
solution: The changes occur together, so the record cannot isolate duration’s contribution.
Record the different changes and relevant conditions; do not claim one caused the outcome.
A qualified review must consider suitability before any real adjustment.

practice.prompt: A fictional log records a better score alongside greater effort and poorer sleep. A report concludes the plan is definitely suitable. Evaluate.
hints: A score is not the only relevant evidence.
solution: A better score alone does not establish the plan’s suitability.
Effort and sleep changes warrant attention but do not establish their cause; other circumstances may matter.
Discuss concerns with an appropriate adult or professional and review the plan rather than automatically increasing demand.

checklist: I distinguish analysis from personal prescription.

lessons.summary: Explain how muscles, breathing and circulation support movement while interpreting simple supplied measurements without diagnosing health or prescribing effort.
objectives: Connect body systems during activity.
Calculate a rate with clear units.
Distinguish an observation from a health conclusion.
explanation: Movement depends on interacting systems. Skeletal muscles generate force, while circulation transports oxygen and nutrients and carries substances such as carbon dioxide away from tissues. Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs, where gases are exchanged with the blood. During activity the demands on these systems can change, but a single heart-rate or breathing observation does not reveal every process involved. Rate describes events per unit time, not the total amount of work done or a person’s overall fitness.

Interpret measurements in their stated conditions. A short pulse count can be converted into an estimated beats-per-minute rate if the rhythm during that interval is representative; counting errors and changing rates limit the estimate. The supplied cases are fictional data exercises, not a request to perform exertion or measure classmates. They provide no diagnosis, target heart rate or personal training prescription. Actual activity and health concerns should follow appropriate school and professional guidance.
keyIdeas: Body systems interact during movement.
Rate calculations require a time unit.
One measurement does not establish a diagnosis or fitness ranking.

definitions.meaning: The number of heartbeats per unit time, commonly per minute.
Movement of air into and out of the lungs.
Muscle tissue that contributes to movement and postural control through force generation.

method: Identify the body systems relevant to the question.
Read the measurement conditions and time interval.
Convert rates using consistent units.
Explain the result and limits without diagnosing the person.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional count: 18 pulses are recorded over 15 seconds. Estimate the rate per minute and state one limitation.
steps: One minute contains four intervals of 15 seconds.
Calculate 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.
State that this estimates the rate from the sampled interval.
A changing pulse or counting error can affect the estimate; the number alone does not diagnose health.
workedExample.conclusion: The estimated rate is 72 beats per minute under the stated assumption, with no individual health conclusion.

misconceptions.mistake: A faster heart rate proves greater fitness.
misconceptions.correction: Interpret rate in context; one value cannot rank overall fitness.

misconceptions.mistake: Breathing and cellular respiration are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical processes in cells.

practice.prompt: Explain different roles of breathing and circulation in supplying working muscles with oxygen.
hints: Connect gas exchange and transport.
solution: Breathing moves air for gas exchange in the lungs.
Circulation carries oxygen in the blood towards tissues, including working muscles; the processes are connected but not identical.

practice.prompt: Original fictional data: 30 pulses are counted in 20 seconds. Estimate beats per minute and explain why it is not a fitness score.
hints: Scale the time interval to one minute.
solution: 60 / 20 = 3, so 30 × 3 = 90 beats per minute.
The estimate depends on the sampled interval and counting accuracy; activity, context and individual factors prevent treating it as an overall fitness score.

practice.prompt: Two fictional pulse readings were taken after different activities using different counting intervals. A learner concludes one person is healthier. Evaluate.
hints: The comparison lacks matched conditions and diagnostic evidence.
solution: The activities and measurement conditions differ, and a pulse reading alone does not establish general health.
Check methods and context for an educational comparison without diagnosing either person.
Any actual health concern requires appropriate qualified support rather than a class ranking.

checklist: I avoid diagnosing from class data.

lessons.summary: Describe movement through joints, force and coordination, using observable evidence while recognising the limits of a written description or single camera view.
objectives: Describe a movement precisely.
Connect muscle action with joint movement.
Distinguish observation from a coaching or health judgement.
explanation: A movement description identifies what changes at a joint or in the body’s position rather than simply calling an action good or bad. Skeletal muscles generate pulling forces and can contribute to movement, resisting movement or maintaining a position. Different muscle groups coordinate a movement; a simplified account of one muscle’s role should not imply that all other muscles are inactive. Balance and control also depend on the task and available support.

Use a relevant observation point and agreed criteria. A single camera angle can hide movement, depth or contact with the surface, so do not infer a complete technique assessment from one image. These exercises use fictional descriptions and do not require you to attempt unfamiliar movements, force a range of motion or diagnose an injury. Practical activity needs appropriate instruction, accessible options and a safe space; written answers cannot demonstrate physical technique.
keyIdeas: Describe the action before judging it.
Muscles can produce force without visible movement.
Camera and task conditions affect the evidence.

definitions.meaning: A connection between bones that may permit movement.
A movement that decreases the angle at a joint, with anatomical conventions depending on the joint.
Organisation of body actions to carry out a task.

method: Identify the task and observable movement.
Name the relevant joint or body relationship.
Explain a possible force or coordination role.
State observation limits and seek appropriate practical guidance.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional description: a person holds a light object still with the elbow bent. A learner says the arm muscles cannot be working because nothing moves. Explain.
steps: Identify the stationary position as the observation.
The object and limb still experience forces including gravity.
Muscle force can help maintain the position without producing visible joint movement.
The description does not reveal exact muscle forces or establish a personal exercise recommendation.
workedExample.conclusion: No visible motion does not imply no muscular force; the holding task still involves postural control.

misconceptions.mistake: Muscles only work when the body visibly moves.
misconceptions.correction: They can generate force while maintaining or resisting a position.

misconceptions.mistake: One camera view proves a movement is safe for everyone.
misconceptions.correction: Safety and technique depend on the person, task and appropriate assessment.

practice.prompt: In a fictional movement description the angle at an elbow decreases as the forearm approaches the upper arm. Name the movement and separate description from quality.
hints: Name the joint action first.
solution: The described elbow movement is flexion.
That label describes the action; it does not by itself show whether the technique is appropriate or safe for a particular person.

practice.prompt: Why might a side-view recording be insufficient to judge whether a moving person also shifts sideways?
hints: A two-dimensional view can hide another direction.
solution: The camera projects movement onto its image plane and can obscure depth or sideways relationships depending on orientation.
Use an appropriate additional view and clear criteria before making a full movement claim, with consent and privacy respected.

practice.prompt: A learner copies an advanced balance position from a video and proposes pushing a classmate into the same shape to improve technique. Evaluate the plan.
hints: Practical learning must respect safety and individual differences.
solution: Do not force another person’s movement or range.
Use qualified instruction, consent, accessible alternatives and a clear safe space.
A video model does not establish suitability for every learner; analyse the movement in writing while seeking appropriate practical guidance.

lessons.summary: Explain the roles of varied foods and interpret basic food information without turning a classroom example into a restrictive diet or personal prescription.
objectives: Recognise that foods provide multiple nutrients.
Compare like-for-like label information.
Consider access, culture and individual needs.
explanation: Food supports growth, everyday activity and health through a range of nutrients. Carbohydrates and fats contribute energy, protein supports structural and functional roles, and vitamins and minerals are needed in smaller amounts. Foods usually contain more than one nutrient, so a food is not simply “a protein” or “a carbohydrate”. A varied, adequate pattern matters more than declaring one ingredient universally good or bad.

Food choices also depend on availability, culture, preference, allergies and individual needs. When interpreting a label, check whether figures refer to a portion or a standard amount before comparing products. These original fictional label exercises teach reasoning rather than calorie restriction, weight change or a meal plan. They do not establish personal nutrient requirements or recommend supplements. Actual allergy, nutrition or growth concerns should be discussed with an appropriate trusted adult or qualified health professional.
keyIdeas: Foods can contribute several nutrients.
Comparisons need the same quantity basis.
Adequacy and diversity matter alongside individual circumstances.

definitions.meaning: A substance used by the body for functions such as energy transfer, growth or regulation.
The amount of a food considered or served on an occasion.
Including different suitable foods across an overall eating pattern.

method: Identify the information and its quantity basis.
Distinguish a nutrient amount from a complete health judgement.
Compare equivalent quantities if a comparison is needed.
Consider the wider pattern and individual constraints without prescribing.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional label: a food contains 6 g of protein per 100 g. Calculate protein in a 50 g portion, without judging whether that portion meets anyone’s daily needs.
steps: The portion is half of the stated 100 g quantity.
Calculate 6 × 50 / 100 = 3 g.
State the unit and portion: 3 g protein in 50 g of this fictional food.
The amount alone does not establish overall diet quality or an individual requirement.
workedExample.conclusion: The portion supplies 3 g of protein according to the fictional label; no personalised intake target is inferred.

misconceptions.mistake: One food supplies only one nutrient.
misconceptions.correction: Most foods contain a mixture of nutrients.

misconceptions.mistake: A single nutrient figure decides whether an entire diet is healthy.
misconceptions.correction: Consider the wider eating pattern, adequacy and individual needs.

practice.prompt: Why is it incomplete to call beans “only protein” in a food lesson?
hints: A food can contain several useful components.
solution: Beans can contribute protein, carbohydrate, fibre and other nutrients.
Describing only one component ignores the food’s broader composition and the rest of the eating pattern.

practice.prompt: Original fictional label: 8 g of fibre per 100 g. How much fibre is in a 25 g portion? State why comparing this directly with another food’s per-100-g figure would be misleading.
hints: Use a common quantity basis.
solution: 8 × 25 / 100 = 2 g of fibre in the 25 g portion.
A portion figure and a per-100-g figure use different denominators; compare equivalent quantities and avoid inferring total diet quality from fibre alone.

practice.prompt: A fictional influencer says every adolescent should remove an entire food group to perform better, without knowing allergies, access or health needs. Evaluate the claim.
hints: Universal restrictive advice needs scrutiny.
solution: The claim ignores growth, adequacy and individual circumstances and provides no relevant evidence for everyone.
Use credible general guidance about varied adequate eating rather than adopting a restrictive plan from the claim.
Specific needs or concerns belong with appropriate qualified support; do not prescribe a replacement diet in this exercise.

checklist: I distinguish education from personal advice.

lessons.summary: Consider physical, emotional and social influences on wellbeing and supportive responses without diagnosing someone or presenting one habit as a cure.
objectives: Recognise interacting influences.
Distinguish support from diagnosis.
Propose respectful and accessible actions.
explanation: Wellbeing includes how people function and experience their lives across physical, emotional and social circumstances. Activity, rest, relationships and opportunities to learn can be relevant, but no single habit guarantees wellbeing or explains every difficulty. Consider the person’s circumstances and access to support rather than treating a struggling learner as simply lacking discipline. A change in behaviour can prompt a caring conversation without proving a particular condition.

Support should respect privacy and choice. Listen without demanding personal disclosures, and involve a trusted adult or appropriate professional when concerns need more support. General activities such as connecting with others or choosing enjoyable accessible movement may support wellbeing; they are not a substitute for care or a promised treatment. The cases here are fictional classroom reasoning exercises, and the answer box should not be used to collect classmates’ private health information.
keyIdeas: Wellbeing has interacting influences.
Observable behaviour does not establish a diagnosis.
Support should be respectful, accessible and proportionate.

definitions.meaning: A broad consideration of how people feel, function and relate within their circumstances.
People and services someone can approach for appropriate help.
Keeping personal information within appropriate agreed boundaries.

method: Describe the concern without labelling the person.
Consider several possible influences and missing information.
Offer respectful choices and appropriate support.
Avoid diagnosis, forced disclosure or promises of a cure.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional case: a classmate has become quieter during a busy assessment period. Suggest a supportive response without diagnosing them.
steps: Treat being quieter as an observation, not proof of a condition.
Ask privately and gently how they are doing, allowing them not to disclose.
Offer practical support or connection with a trusted adult if they want or need it.
Do not promise that a single activity will solve the difficulty.
workedExample.conclusion: A caring response acknowledges uncertainty and access to support rather than assigning a diagnosis.

misconceptions.mistake: A person’s appearance reveals their wellbeing.
misconceptions.correction: Ask respectfully and avoid assumptions from appearance or one behaviour.

misconceptions.mistake: Exercise alone cures every mental-health difficulty.
misconceptions.correction: Activity may support wellbeing but does not replace appropriate care.

practice.prompt: Distinguish “Sam missed two club meetings” from “Sam definitely has a mental-health condition.”
hints: Separate observation and diagnosis.
solution: Missing meetings is the stated observation.
A condition is not established; many circumstances could explain the absence. Offer a respectful check-in rather than a label.

practice.prompt: A fictional school wellbeing activity assumes everyone enjoys competitive running. Suggest two inclusive changes without prescribing exercise to individuals.
hints: Offer choice and different ways to participate.
solution: Offer accessible, non-competitive options and ways to connect or contribute that suit different needs.
Ask participants what supports participation without demanding private medical details, and use appropriate school guidance.

practice.prompt: A poster claims one breathing activity will remove all stress and that anyone who still struggles is not trying. Evaluate and rewrite the message.
hints: Avoid a guaranteed cure and blame.
solution: The claim overpromises and unfairly blames people whose circumstances differ.
A calm activity may help some people; it is one possible support, not a guaranteed solution.
Encourage seeking a trusted adult or appropriate professional when difficulties persist or require help.

checklist: I know when more support is needed.

lessons.summary: Explain how a team can choose and revise a plan in response to space, rules, opponents and opportunities for inclusive participation.
objectives: Distinguish a general strategy from an immediate tactical decision.
Explain a decision using the stated game situation.
Evaluate a plan using more than the final score.
explanation: A strategy is an overall approach to a game problem, such as keeping possession by offering several passing options. A tactic is a particular action used in a situation, such as moving into an available space to become a passing option. The usefulness of either depends on the rules, space, participants and what opponents do. A plan that worked once is not automatically the best answer in a different situation.

Analyse decisions with evidence about opportunities as well as outcomes. A well-chosen option can still fail through execution or an opponent’s response, while a poor decision can occasionally succeed. In a learning setting, consider whether the rules and roles enable everyone to contribute. These original fictional scenarios develop decision reasoning; they are not instructions to perform an unsupervised sport or proof of practical competence. Any real activity needs appropriate instruction, suitable conditions and accessible choices.
keyIdeas: Strategies depend on context.
Decisions and outcomes are related but different.
Participation is part of evaluating a learning game.

definitions.meaning: An overall approach to achieving an aim in a game.
A specific action selected in response to a situation.
An available way for a teammate to continue play within the rules.

method: Identify the objective and stated rules.
Describe the available options and constraints.
Explain one choice and its likely trade-off.
Review observations and propose a contextual adjustment.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional non-contact passing game: three teammates crowd one marked space and passes are often intercepted. Propose a strategy and a way to judge it.
steps: Identify the objective as keeping possession within the agreed rules.
Suggest offering separated passing options rather than crowding one position.
Explain that this may create clearer options but opponents can respond.
Compare available options, participation and interceptions across comparable observations.
workedExample.conclusion: Creating useful space is a reasoned proposal, not a guaranteed scoring method; review evidence and accessibility.

misconceptions.mistake: Winning proves every decision was good.
misconceptions.correction: Examine the decisions, conditions and contributions as well as the result.

misconceptions.mistake: One tactic suits every game.
misconceptions.correction: Rules, participants and opponents change which options are useful.

practice.prompt: Distinguish “keep possession by offering several options” from “move to the open left space now” in a fictional passing game.
hints: Compare overall approach and immediate action.
solution: The first is an overall strategy for keeping possession.
The second is a tactical action responding to the available space.

practice.prompt: In an original case, a team wins but two players never receive a pass. Explain why the score alone cannot establish successful inclusive participation.
hints: Consider evidence about involvement.
solution: The win records the scoring result, not everyone’s participation.
Review opportunities to contribute, roles and player feedback; consider suitable rule or space changes with the teacher.

practice.prompt: A team says one successful long pass proves long passes are always best. Evaluate and propose a fair next observation.
hints: One event does not establish a universal strategy.
solution: The pass succeeded in one situation; distance alone does not explain its usefulness.
Compare decisions when passing options, opponent positions and rules are recorded.
Retain unsuccessful attempts and assess whether alternatives were available.

lessons.summary: Use defined observations and comparable denominators to describe performance while separating evidence from causes and personal judgements.
objectives: Define an observable performance measure.
Calculate a success rate with its denominator.
Explain the limits of a comparison.
explanation: Performance analysis starts with a question and a clear definition of what will be observed. “Successful passes divided by attempted passes” is interpretable only when success and an attempt are defined consistently. Record the situation, observation period and any missing events. Video, where appropriately authorised, can help revisit a decision, but a camera view may hide relevant information. A numerical result describes the recorded sample; it is not a measure of a person’s worth or overall health.

Compare like conditions before suggesting improvement. Different opponents, rules, observation lengths or types of attempts can change a result. A larger number of successes may come from more opportunities, so inspect both counts and rates. Keep uncertainty visible and use specific, respectful feedback tied to an observation. The fictional records here require no learner recordings or private health data. They cannot establish that a training method caused a change or replace a teacher’s observation of practical skills.
keyIdeas: Measures need definitions and denominators.
Context changes comparisons.
Observation alone does not establish cause.

definitions.meaning: The number meeting a stated success definition divided by the number of eligible attempts.
Agreed definitions and procedures for recording events.
A difference that can affect a comparison and complicate a causal explanation.

method: Define the measure and eligible attempts.
Record successes, attempts and context.
Calculate the rate using the matching denominator.
State limitations before proposing feedback.

workedExample.prompt: Fictional logs: A records 12 successful passes from 20 attempts; B records 15 from 30 under different opponents. Compare.
steps: B has more successes but a lower recorded success rate.
Different opponents prevent attributing the difference solely to the player or a training change.
workedExample.conclusion: The recorded rates are 60% and 50%; causal and general performance claims remain limited.

misconceptions.mistake: More successes always means a higher success rate.
misconceptions.correction: Compare successes with the number of attempts.

misconceptions.mistake: A changed rate proves what caused the change.
misconceptions.correction: Check conditions and alternative explanations before a causal claim.

practice.prompt: An original observation log records 9 successful attempts out of 12. Calculate the success rate.
hints: Divide successes by attempts.

practice.prompt: Fictional logs show A: 8 successes in 10 attempts; B: 12 in 20. Compare counts and rates.
hints: Calculate each fraction before judging.
solution: B has more successes: 12 rather than 8.
A has the higher recorded rate: 80% compared with 60%.
Neither comparison alone establishes overall ability without context.

practice.prompt: A school report credits a new strategy for an improved pass rate, but the second observation used easier opposition and excluded failed attempts. Evaluate.
hints: Examine comparability and selection.
solution: The opposition changed, so the observations are not directly comparable.
Excluding failures biases the rate and changes the denominator.
Retain all eligible attempts, specify conditions and avoid claiming the strategy caused the change from these records.

checklist: I give specific and qualified feedback.

lessons.summary: Evaluate the logic and missing information in a fictional activity plan without turning a classroom example into a personal exercise prescription.
objectives: Relate a plan’s stated activities to its stated aim.
Identify missing recovery, access and review information.
Separate planning analysis from approval to perform activity.
explanation: A training plan connects an aim with activity choices, scheduling, recovery and a way to review what happened. Classroom analysis can ask whether those elements agree without deciding what an individual should do. A list of difficult activities is not automatically an effective plan. Its suitability depends on the person, prior experience, support and conditions, and on factors that a short worksheet may not describe. Do not infer readiness from age, appearance or a single performance number.

Review a plan as a proposal with uncertainty. Look for an appropriate starting point, a rationale for any change, space for recovery and a process for adjusting when circumstances change. There is no universal percentage increase that makes every activity suitable. Real participation should follow qualified instruction and relevant school guidance, with accessible alternatives and a way to raise concerns. The original fictional examples below practise critique and documentation; their numbers and schedules are not a programme for the learner to follow.
keyIdeas: A plan needs an aim and a review process.
Suitability requires individual context and appropriate guidance.
More activity is not automatically better.

definitions.meaning: An explanation linking proposed choices to an aim and relevant evidence.
A planned opportunity to compare observations and reconsider the proposal.
A considered change in response to evidence, needs or circumstances.

method: State the fictional aim and available information.
Check how proposed choices connect to that aim.
Identify missing suitability, recovery and access information.
Recommend a review process without prescribing an individual workload.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional worksheet proposes hard running every day to improve a learner’s passing decisions, gives no starting information and says never change the schedule. Critique the plan.
steps: Passing decisions require relevant decision evidence; hard running alone does not establish that learning.
The worksheet omits prior experience, suitability and appropriate instruction.
A rigid schedule without recovery or a way to report concerns is not adequately justified.
Ask a qualified teacher to review an inclusive proposal and specify observations that would prompt revision.
workedExample.conclusion: The proposal is insufficiently justified; this critique does not supply or approve an individual exercise programme.

misconceptions.mistake: A fixed percentage increase is suitable for everyone.
misconceptions.correction: Changes depend on individual context, activity and qualified guidance.

misconceptions.mistake: Following a plan means ignoring all new information.
misconceptions.correction: A useful plan includes review and appropriate adjustment.

practice.prompt: A fictional plan lists activities but no aim or review point. Identify two missing planning elements and explain their purpose.
hints: Connect choices and evidence.
solution: An aim explains what the plan is intended to develop.
A review point identifies when and how observations will inform a revision.

practice.prompt: A fictional plan promises better team communication solely by increasing running distance. Explain the gap without writing a personal workout.
hints: Match the measure and activity to the aim.
solution: More distance does not by itself demonstrate communication learning.
The plan needs relevant communication opportunities and observations, suitable participation conditions and qualified review.

practice.prompt: An online template says everyone should increase every session by the same percentage and ignore pain to show commitment. Evaluate this advice.
hints: Uniform workload rules cannot establish individual suitability.
solution: A universal increase ignores different experience, activities and circumstances.
Pain should not be treated as a commitment test; stop the painful activity and seek appropriate adult or professional guidance.
A real plan needs qualified oversight, suitable recovery and an agreed review process, not pressure to continue.

checklist: I connect choices with an aim.
I do not treat a worksheet as personal approval.

lessons.summary: Use recorded evidence to explain learning, recognise limits and choose a relevant next question without inventing practical achievements.
objectives: Distinguish description from evidence-based reflection.
Discuss improvements and unresolved difficulties.
Propose a next check linked to the evidence.
explanation: Reflection explains what an experience or record suggests about learning and what remains uncertain. A description states what happened; reflection connects an observation with a goal, considers possible explanations and identifies a reasoned next step. Use actual records when discussing real activity. If the task supplies a fictional case, keep the response within that case rather than claiming you performed it. A positive tone does not require hiding missed goals or untested skills.

Consider performance, decisions and participation separately. A result may improve while a communication goal remains unmet, or practical execution may remain uncertain despite a clear written explanation. Recognise assistance and changes in conditions that limit comparison. A next step should respond to a specific gap and remain subject to appropriate instruction and suitability. These model responses assess classroom reasoning only; completing them does not certify fitness, health, safe technique or readiness for a particular activity.
keyIdeas: Reflection connects evidence to a goal.
Mixed outcomes can be reported honestly.
Written reasoning does not certify practical performance.

definitions.meaning: An interpretation of learning supported by specified evidence.
Information needed for a judgement but not yet available.
A focused way to obtain evidence relevant to an unresolved question.

method: Name the goal and relevant record.
Explain what the evidence supports.
Retain uncertainty and alternative explanations.
Propose a relevant next check with appropriate support.

workedExample.prompt: Original case: a group sought more shared decisions. Its log records suggestions from two of five members before and four of five after a rule change. The second session also used a different teacher prompt. Reflect.
steps: The recorded number contributing suggestions rose from two to four members.
This supports a limited claim of broader recorded contribution in those sessions.
It does not show every contribution influenced decisions or isolate the rule change from the teacher prompt.
Review how suggestions were used and gather voluntary feedback while recording comparable conditions.
workedExample.conclusion: The evidence suggests a participation change, with unresolved questions about influence and cause.

misconceptions.mistake: Reflection must prove complete success.
misconceptions.correction: Include unresolved difficulties and evidence that does not fit the goal.

misconceptions.mistake: A strong written response proves safe practical execution.
misconceptions.correction: Practical competence needs appropriate observation and assessment.

practice.prompt: A learner writes “We played and it was good.” Identify what would make this a more useful reflection.
hints: Add a goal, observation and interpretation.
solution: Name the goal and a specific recorded observation.
Explain what that observation suggests and identify an unresolved question or next check.

practice.prompt: In a fictional case, pass rate rises from 50% to 60%, but two teammates still receive no passes. Reflect on performance and participation separately.
hints: Do not let one measure stand for every goal.
solution: The recorded pass rate improved by 10 percentage points under the stated observations.
That does not establish inclusive participation; two teammates still received none.
Review opportunities and roles as well as the conditions behind the rate comparison.

practice.prompt: After completing written movement questions, a learner claims certified safe technique in a real sport. Evaluate and identify missing evidence.
hints: Separate explanation and practical assessment.
solution: Written answers demonstrate reasoning within the task, not certified practical performance.
Relevant technique needs appropriate supervised observation and assessment in context.
Do not invent that observation or recommend an unsupervised test to fill the gap.

checklist: I propose a relevant next check.
